justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline for what appears to be an equity index or ETF trading near the 515–520 range. For the 1-day estimate of 515.5, I was essentially anchoring near the last observed price with a very slight upward drift, reflecting the general positive expected return of equities over any given day combined with mean-reversion tendencies in the short run. The 1-week estimate of 517 incorporates a small additional drift premium while acknowledging that intraweek volatility tends to wash out directional signals. The 1-month estimate of 522 reflects a slightly more pronounced trend assumption — roughly consistent with annualized equity returns in the 6–8% range — while remaining conservative enough to avoid overconfidence in any particular directional move over a 30-day window.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily around historical realized volatility. At the 1-day horizon, the tight 505–526 band (roughly ±2%) reflects typical daily price swings for a broad equity instrument. At 1 week, the band widens to ±roughly 3.5% to account for the compounding of daily uncertainty and the possibility of a macro surprise mid-week. At 1 month, the 485–560 range represents a ±roughly 7% envelope, which is consistent with one standard deviation of monthly returns for a moderately volatile equity instrument. Liquidity conditions, time of month, and whether we are in an earnings season window also subtly influenced how wide I set these bands.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals include unexpected central bank policy shifts — particularly from the Federal Reserve — which have historically caused single-day moves of 3–5% in equity markets. Geopolitical escalations, a surprise inflation print, or a major corporate earnings miss from a systemically important company could all generate tail moves. On the upside, a sudden de-escalation of trade tensions, a stronger-than-expected employment report, or a dovish pivot signal could push prices well above my 1-month upper bound of 560.

It is also worth noting that my intervals carry model risk themselves. I assumed roughly stationary volatility, but volatility is known to cluster — if the market enters a high-volatility regime, even my 1-week intervals could prove too narrow. Conversely, if conditions remain unusually calm, realized outcomes may stay tightly clustered around my point estimates. Readers should treat these intervals as reasonable but imperfect guides rather than precise probability envelopes.
